opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that people don't come to an image model with one neat, predefined task. They come with a messy, evolving idea. Maybe they start by generating something from scratch, then they want to change the lighting, then swap out the background, then put their own face or their dog into the scene, then fix a little detail. If you have a separate specialized model for each of those steps, the user has to know which tool to reach for and stitch everything together themselves, and that's a lot of friction.

By making it one general model that understands both generation and editing, and that you can just talk to in natural language, the interaction becomes conversational. You iterate. You say "now make it nighttime" or "keep the character the same but put them on a bike," and it just does it. That consistency across edits, keeping a person or an object looking like itself as you change everything around it, turned out to be something people really cared about, and it falls out much more naturally when one model is reasoning about the whole image and the whole conversation.

The other thing is that generality lets people surprise us. We had ideas about what the main use cases would be, but once it was out there, people found all kinds of things we hadn't anticipated: restoring old family photos, making figurines of themselves, visualizing home renovations, creating little comics, educational diagrams. A narrow model would have capped that creativity. A general one lets the community discover the use cases, and that kind of grassroots discovery and sharing is really what drove a lot of the adoption.

And finally, building on top of a strong multimodal language model means it brings along a lot of world knowledge and instruction-following. So it's not just pushing pixels around. It understands what you're asking for, which makes it feel less like operating software and more like collaborating with someone.

r001.rationale: The response links adoption to a general model that handles both image generation and editing, reducing friction and supporting conversational iteration.

r002.rationale: It says developers had expected use cases, but users discovered unanticipated ones, and that grassroots discovery and sharing drove adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the general-purpose part is actually the whole story in a lot of ways. When we were building it, there was a real temptation to go narrow, to say, okay, let's build the best possible background remover, or the best possible headshot generator, because those are well-defined problems and you can measure them cleanly. But what we kept seeing in the research was that image editing isn't really one problem. It's a thousand little problems that people have, and most of them don't fit neatly into a dropdown menu.

So the bet was, if you build a model that understands images and understands language well enough that you can just describe what you want, then you don't have to anticipate the use cases in advance. And that turned out to matter a lot for adoption, because the use cases people actually came up with were not the ones we would have prioritized. People were restoring old family photos, they were putting themselves into scenes with their pets, they were doing product mockups for tiny businesses, they were making figurines of themselves, that whole trend. None of that was on a roadmap. It emerged because the model was flexible enough to let people try things.

The other piece is that generality lowers the barrier to trying it at all. If I have to learn a tool, or learn which mode to pick, there's friction. If I can just upload a picture and say "make it look like it was taken at golden hour and take my cousin out of the background," and it does both in one shot, that's a very different experience. It feels less like software and more like asking a person. And I think that's what made it spread, honestly. People would do one edit, get a result that surprised them, and immediately want to show somebody.

And then there's a compounding effect on the research side too. When you're training one model to do editing, generation, multi-image composition, character consistency, all of those things, the capabilities reinforce each other. The consistency you need for editing makes generation better. The world knowledge you need for generation makes editing more sensible. So the general model ends up being better at each individual task than a specialized one might have been, which is a little counterintuitive, but it's what we found.

r001.rationale: The response says the model’s flexible, general-purpose capabilities helped adoption by letting users try many edits without choosing a specialized tool or mode.

r002.rationale: It says users’ popular uses—such as restoring family photos, making pet scenes, and creating figurines—were not anticipated or on the developers’ roadmap.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that people don’t think about their problems in terms of separate image generation and image editing tasks. They have something they want to create, and then they want to change it. Having one model that supports that whole process makes it much easier to get started and keep iterating.

You can start with a prompt, or you can bring an image you already have and describe what you want to do with it. That opens up a lot of different uses without requiring people to learn a specialized workflow for each one.

And that generality gives people room to discover things themselves. You don’t have to anticipate every use case. People try something, share what worked, and that gives someone else an idea. I think that kind of experimentation is a really powerful driver of adoption.

r001.rationale: It links adoption to one model supporting both creating and changing images, making it easier to start and iterate.

r002.rationale: It says users can discover uses the developers did not anticipate, but does not state that any publicly popular uses were unanticipated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that people don’t have to translate what they want into a very specialized workflow. They can bring an image, describe a change in natural language, and then keep iterating. And if they don’t have an image to start with, they can generate one in the same place.

That opens it up to a much broader set of use cases. Someone might use it for something playful, discover that it works well, and then realize they can also use it for a presentation or a creative project. You don’t have to anticipate every application as the model builder. Giving people a general-purpose capability lets them discover uses that you wouldn’t necessarily have thought of.

r001.rationale: It links adoption to broad, general-purpose editing and generation that lets people describe changes, iterate, and use the model across many applications.

r002.rationale: It says people may discover uses the builders did not anticipate, but does not say those uses became publicly popular.
